annotation_description: Playing Undercity Sewers (which enters tapped) instead of Scalding Tarn on turn 1 is a significant mistake. With Scalding Tarn, they could fetch Underground Sea (untapped), giving them access to mana on turn 1. Combined with Lotus Petal and Dark Ritual, this enables casting Orcish Bowmasters or even setting up for Quantum Riddler via Warp. More importantly, Scalding Tarn + Lotus Petal + Dark Ritual = BBB + one from petal = potential turn 1 plays. With Undercity Sewers entering tapped, they have zero mana available this turn. Additionally, having Daze in hand means they want an Island they can return — Scalding Tarn fetching an Island is better for Daze. Playing the tapped land first also means on turn 2 they'd have the Sewers untapped plus could play Scalding Tarn, but the tempo loss of not having mana available turn 1 when holding Dark Ritual and Lotus Petal is meaningful. The correct line is likely Scalding Tarn, fetch Underground Sea, then potentially cast Lotus Petal and have options open including holding up Daze with a bounceable Island.

The opponent cast Dark Ritual on turn 1, which likely enables a powerful follow-up play (possibly Orcish Bowmasters or another threat). GLM47 had both Daze and Force of Will available to counter it. Daze could be cast for free by returning the tapped Undercity Sewers to hand (it's an Island), which would counter Dark Ritual unless the opponent pays {1} (unlikely on turn 1). Force of Will could be cast by exiling Quantum Riddler (a blue card) and paying 1 life. Letting Dark Ritual resolve gives the opponent 3 black mana on turn 1, enabling explosive plays. Daze is particularly efficient here since the Undercity Sewers is already tapped and the opponent likely can't pay {1} on turn 1. The cost of bouncing the land is minimal since it enters tapped anyway and can be replayed.

Casting Ponder before playing Undercity Sewers is a sequencing error. Undercity Sewers enters tapped and triggers surveil 1, which would let them bin a card before Ponder. This provides additional information for the Ponder decision and fuels Murktide Regent's delve. The land enters tapped so it doesn't affect mana availability this turn.

When ordering cards for Ponder, the player chose to put Barrowgoyf on the bottom (it will be drawn first since the last chosen goes on top) and Orcish Bowmasters on top. However, the player already has two Orcish Bowmasters in hand. Barrowgoyf would likely be a better draw since the opponent has cards in the graveyard (Lotus Petal, Dark Ritual) making it immediately relevant as a threat, and the player already has redundant copies of Bowmasters. That said, a third Bowmasters could still be useful. The ordering here puts Barrowgoyf as the card drawn (first chosen = bottom of the two, which is drawn first after Ponder draws), and Bowmasters on top for next turn. Actually, let me re-read: 'last one chosen will be topmost'. So Barrowgoyf was chosen first (goes second from top), then the remaining card Orcish Bowmasters would be placed on top. Wait - there are only 2 choices and the player chose Barrowgoyf. This means Barrowgoyf goes on bottom of the two, Orcish Bowmasters goes on top. Ponder then draws a card, so the player draws Orcish Bowmasters (the topmost card). Given the player already has 2 Bowmasters in hand, drawing a third is less valuable than drawing Barrowgoyf which would be a unique threat. The player should have put Orcish Bowmasters on bottom and Barrowgoyf on top to draw Barrowgoyf.

Casting Consider before activating Scalding Tarn is a sequencing error. The correct line is to activate Scalding Tarn first, which shuffles the library, and then cast Consider. This way, if the top card revealed by Consider is undesirable, you've already used your shuffle effect. By casting Consider first, you surveil 1 and draw, but if the top card was bad, you've lost the option to shuffle with Scalding Tarn before drawing. Additionally, fetching first would thin the deck slightly before the surveil/draw. Furthermore, casting Consider into an opponent with an untapped Underground Sea is risky if they have Daze (though they tapped it), but more importantly the opponent could have Orcish Bowmasters which punishes the extra draw. However, the opponent's Underground Sea is tapped, so the Bowmasters concern is less immediate. The sequencing issue with fetch-before-cantrip is the main problem.

GLM47 is using Daze to counter Consider, which is a cheap cantrip. This requires bouncing an Island (Undercity Sewers or fetching first), setting back their mana development on turn 2. Daze is a valuable tempo counter that's much better used against more impactful spells. Consider is a 1-mana cantrip - trading Daze + a land drop for it is a poor exchange. The opponent has only 1 land (Underground Sea, tapped) and no cards that suggest an immediate threat. GLM47's hand contains Quantum Riddler which needs mana to cast (even with Warp at {1}{U}), and Force of Will as a backup counter for truly important spells. Bouncing their own land to counter a cantrip delays their own development significantly while the opponent loses very little.

annotation_description: GLM47 is casting Daze targeting opponent's Consider. Daze costs {1}{U} if paid normally. GLM47 has Undercity Sewers (tapped) and Scalding Tarn available. To pay {1}{U} normally, they'd need to crack Scalding Tarn for an Island (paying 1 life) and tap Undercity Sewers - but Undercity Sewers is already tapped. They likely can't even pay the mana cost. Meanwhile, the alternative cost of returning an Island (Undercity Sewers) to hand is free mana-wise. Returning Undercity Sewers to hand is a real cost (losing a land drop temporarily), but paying {1}{U} when you only have Scalding Tarn untapped means you'd need to crack the fetch, losing it permanently AND paying 1 life, just to counter a Consider. The alternative cost preserves Scalding Tarn on the battlefield and only temporarily sets back the land (you can replay Undercity Sewers next turn). More importantly, countering Consider with Daze at full mana cost is a terrible trade - spending 2 mana and cracking a fetchland to counter a 1-mana cantrip, when the alternative cost lets you do it for free (just bouncing a land). This is especially bad because GLM47's hand is Force of Will and Quantum Riddler - they need lands to eventually cast Quantum Riddler or its Warp cost.

message: Select a blue card from your hand
annotation_description: Exiled Quantum Riddler (which has Warp {1}{U}, a realistic 2-mana casting cost) instead of Daze to pay for Force of Will. With only 1 land on board, Daze's alternate cost of bouncing that land is very painful, making Daze less valuable. Quantum Riddler could realistically be cast as early as turn 3 via Warp and would provide a meaningful threat plus card advantage.

Casting Thoughtseize before playing a land for turn is a sequencing error. The opponent has only 1 card in hand, so Thoughtseize's value is limited (might whiff on a land). More importantly, by casting Thoughtseize first with Underground Sea, they use their only mana and cannot play Ponder this turn. If they had played Misty Rainforest first (getting a second land), they could have cast both Thoughtseize and Ponder, or at minimum had better mana flexibility. Additionally, playing a fetch land first before Thoughtseize lets you see the opponent's hand and then make a more informed decision about what to fetch. The correct sequence is to play a land first (Misty Rainforest), then decide on spell casting order with 2 mana available.

annotation_description: GLM47 used Daze to counter Thoughtseize when their hand was empty (Daze was the last card). Letting Thoughtseize resolve would have resulted in the opponent seeing an empty hand, discarding nothing, and losing 2 life for no benefit. Instead, GLM47 bounced their own Island, setting back their mana development for no reason.

Fetching Underground Sea instead of a basic Island leaves the player more vulnerable to Wasteland, which is one of the most common cards in Legacy. The player already has one Underground Sea in play, so a second dual land provides no additional color fixing benefit over a basic Island (which also taps for U). Having a basic Island ensures that if the opponent plays Wasteland, the player still has a land that produces mana. With two Underground Seas and no basics, a single Wasteland could be devastating, especially when the player wants to hold up Daze (which requires returning an Island to hand). The player even acknowledges Wasteland concerns in their reasoning but then fetches the dual anyway.

With Ponder, the player is ordering two cards on top of their library. They chose Snuff Out first (which means it goes on bottom, with Wasteland on top). Given the board state, the player has two Orcish Bowmasters and a Murktide Regent in hand but only two lands in play (both Underground Seas) and an Undercity Sewers in hand that enters tapped. Wasteland on top means they draw Wasteland this turn from Ponder. However, Wasteland is less immediately useful than Snuff Out - the opponent only has one tapped Undercity Sewers and no creatures. Snuff Out is a removal spell that can be cast for free (4 life) if they control a Swamp (Underground Sea counts). Having Snuff Out available as the draw would give them interaction against whatever creature the opponent deploys, while Wasteland only threatens the opponent's single dual land. The player should have put Wasteland first (bottom) and Snuff Out second (top) to draw Snuff Out, keeping removal available while they develop their board with Orcish Bowmasters.

Casting Murktide Regent main phase into an opponent with 2 untapped lands (Island + Undercity Sewers providing U/B) when the opponent could potentially have interaction. The opponent's graveyard shows they've already used Force of Will and Daze, but casting a 7-mana threat (even with Delve) before combat and before deploying Orcish Bowmasters seems suboptimal. Bowmasters at flash speed could be held up, and playing Murktide into potential countermagic when you could instead deploy a Bowmasters (which has flash anyway) and hold up Daze protection seems risky. However, Murktide with 4 cards to exile from graveyard (Ponder, Thoughtseize, Misty Rainforest, Ponder) would cost UU + exile 4 cards for a 7/7 flyer paying just 2 mana, which is a massive threat. The opponent has already spent their Force of Will and Daze, so the coast may be relatively clear. Still, leading with the biggest threat when you could sequence Bowmasters first (or hold Murktide to protect with Daze) is debatable.

Casting Orcish Bowmasters during own postcombat main phase instead of holding it up to cast at instant speed during the opponent's turn. Bowmasters has flash and triggers on opponent card draws - casting it on the opponent's turn (e.g., in response to a cantrip or during draw step) would potentially generate an extra damage trigger and amass trigger. The opponent is playing a cantrip-heavy deck.

chosen_display: Wasteland — {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Destroy target nonbasic la... [Activate]
annotation_description: Using Wasteland now destroys the opponent's Undercity Sewers (their only non-basic land), which is reasonable tempo. However, Gem3P has two Orcish Bowmasters in hand and only 2 Underground Seas remaining after sacrificing Wasteland. Playing an Orcish Bowmasters this turn would require both Underground Seas, leaving no mana for Daze's alternate cost (no Island to bounce) or the second Bowmasters next turn without playing the Undercity Sewers (which enters tapped). The Wasteland play cuts Gem3P down to 2 lands with a hand full of spells. An alternative line is to deploy Orcish Bowmasters first (using 1U from the two Underground Seas), then Wasteland the opponent's land on a future turn or hold it as a threat. That said, destroying the opponent's dual land while they only have 2 lands is strong tempo denial, and the opponent's graveyard suggests they may be building toward a Murktide of their own. The sequencing is debatable - Bowmasters now + Wasteland later vs Wasteland now + Bowmasters later both have merits.

Cast Murktide Regent before playing a land for the turn. Playing Swamp first would have left one extra untapped land after casting Murktide (4 lands, only 3 needed with full delve), and crucially would have enabled Snuff Out's alternate cost (pay 4 life) by controlling a Swamp. Casting spells before making the land drop is a sequencing error that gives up free value.

Casting Orcish Bowmasters before activating Wasteland is suboptimal sequencing. By Wastelanding the opponent's Undercity Sewers first (leaving them with only 1 Island), the opponent would be less able to pay for any counterspells or interact. The player has enough remaining mana (2 Underground Seas + Swamp = 3 sources after sacrificing Wasteland) to still cast Bowmasters afterward.

Allowing a second Orcish Bowmasters to resolve makes it extremely difficult to recover, as every cantrip drawn will now deal 2 damage and create 2 amass triggers. With GLM47 already behind on board and needing to cantrip to find threats like Murktide Regent, two Bowmasters essentially locks them out of their primary game plan.

Putting Thoughtseize back on top of the library instead of the second Daze. The opponent has multiple untapped lands (Underground Sea, Swamp), making Daze easy to pay for. Thoughtseize provides hand information and guaranteed disruption, which is more valuable than a second Daze the opponent can pay through.

Gem3P passed without taking any action in precombat main when they could play Island and cast Murktide Regent via Delve (exiling 4 graveyard cards, paying {1}{U}{U}), creating a 6/6 flyer. Combined with the existing board of ~6 power (2 Bowmasters + Orc Army token), this would represent lethal damage against an opponent at 7 life. Even without Murktide, Wasteland on opponent's Undercity Sewers would be valuable.
